{{Short description|American physicist and computer scientist}}
'''Richard E. Crandall''' (December 29, 1947 – December 20, 2012) was an American [[physicist]] and [[computer scientist]] who made contributions to [[computational number theory]].

==Background==
Crandall was born in Ann Arbor, Michigan, and spent two years at [[California Institute of Technology|Caltech]] before transferring to [[Reed College]] in Portland, Oregon, where he graduated in physics and wrote his undergraduate thesis on randomness.<ref name="ReedMag">{{Cite web|url=https://www.reed.edu/reed-magazine/in-memoriam/obituaries/march2013/richard-e-crandall-1969.html|title=Prof. Richard E. Crandall '69|website=Reed Magazine {{!}} In Memoriam|language=en-us|date=March 2013|access-date=June 20, 2019}}</ref> He earned his Ph.D. in theoretical physics from [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]].<ref name="ReedMag"/>

==Career==
In 1978, he became a physics professor at Reed College, where he taught courses in experimental physics and computational physics for many years, ultimately becoming Vollum Professor of Science and director of the Center for Advanced Computation.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://archive.dailycal.org/article/5879/scientists_envision_applications_for_pi_in_encrypt|title=Scientists Envision Applications for Pi In Encrypted Internet Transactions|last=Weege|first=Tez|date=August 10, 2001|work=The Daily Californian|access-date=April 1, 2013|archive-date=April 14, 2013|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130414130434/http://archive.dailycal.org/article/5879/scientists_envision_applications_for_pi_in_encrypt|url-status=dead}}</ref> He was also, at various times, Chief Scientist at [[NeXT]], Inc., Chief Cryptographer and Distinguished Scientist at [[Apple Inc.|Apple]], and head of Apple's Advanced Computation Group.

He was a pioneer in experimental mathematics. He developed the [[irrational base discrete weighted transform]], a method of finding very large primes. He wrote several books and many scholarly papers on scientific programming and computation.

Crandall was awarded numerous patents for his work in the field of [[cryptography]]. He also wrote a poker program that could [[Bluff (poker)|bluff]]. He owned and operated PSI Press, an online publishing company.

==Personal life==
Crandall was part [[Cherokee]] and proud of his Native heritage.<ref name="ReedMag"/> He fronted a band called the Chameleons in 1981.<ref>{{cite news |title=The Chameleons (UK) Frequently Asked Questions (note by Damian Ramsay) |first=Mik |last=Foggin |work=The Chameleons website |date=October 13, 2005 |url=http://www.thechameleons.com/band/faq.php#II21 |access-date=December 13, 2008 |archive-date=September 26, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180926121220/http://www.thechameleons.com/band/faq.php#II21 |url-status=dead }}</ref> He was working on an intellectual biography of Steve Jobs when he collapsed at his home in Portland, Oregon, from acute [[leukemia]]. He died 10 days later, on December 20, 2012, at the age of 64.<ref name="Reed">{{cite news|url=http://www.reed.edu/reed_magazine/sallyportal/posts/2012/prof.-richard-crandall-dead-at-64.html|title=Prof. Richard Crandall dead at 64|last=Lydgate|first=Chris|date=December 20, 2012|work=Reed Magazine|archive-date=January 15, 2013|access-date=December 20, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130115035847/http://www.reed.edu/reed_magazine/sallyportal/posts/2012/prof.-richard-crandall-dead-at-64.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Books==
*''Pascal Applications for the Sciences.'' John Wiley & Sons, New York 1983.
* with M. M. Colgrove: ''Scientific Programming with Macintosh Pascal''. John Wiley & Sons, New York 1986.
* ''Mathematica for the Sciences'', Addison-Wesley, Reading, Mass, 1991.
* ''Projects in Scientific Computation.'' Springer 1994.
*  ''Topics in Advanced Scientific Computation.'' Springer 1996.
* with M. Levich: ''A Network Orange.'' Springer 1997.
* with [[Carl Pomerance|C. Pomerance]]: ''Prime numbers: A Computational Perspective.'' Springer 2001.
